item.title: Oita Events 2026: Beppu Fireworks, Onsen Festival & Usuki Takeyoi
item.description: Oita is Japan’s onsen capital — Beppu and Yufuin between them pour out more hot-spring water than anywhere else in the country — and its 2026 event calendar reflects that steamy character. A spring festival celebrates the hot springs themselves, summer brings fireworks over Beppu Bay, and autumn glows with thousands of bamboo lanterns in a castle town. Add the ever-bubbling “hells” of Beppu, and Oita rewards a well-timed 2026 trip.

item.title: Beppu Onsen Day Trip from Miyazaki — Guide
item.description: While Beppu lies just over the border in Oita prefecture, its fame as Japan’s greatest onsen town makes it a popular addition to a wider Kyushu itinerary that includes Miyazaki. Set on a bay ringed by volcanic mountains, Beppu produces a colossal volume of hot-spring water across eight districts, with columns of white steam constantly rising over the town. Its signature attraction is the ‘Hells of Beppu’ — a tour of vividly coloured hot springs, from a cobalt-blue pool to a blood-red pond, that are for viewing rather than bathing — alongside an incredible variety of baths to soak in: sand baths, mud baths, steam baths and countless open-air rotenburo.

item.title: Oita Kabosu Citrus — Guide
item.description: Kabosu is Oita’s signature citrus fruit, and the prefecture grows the overwhelming majority of Japan’s entire crop. A round, green citrus resembling a large lime, kabosu is prized not for eating whole but for its fragrant, tangy juice, which is squeezed over food much like a lemon or lime but with its own distinctive, refreshing aroma and a milder, more rounded acidity. In Oita it’s a beloved everyday condiment: a squeeze of kabosu brightens grilled fish and sashimi, the region’s famous Seki-saba and Seki-aji, Bungo beef, toriten, hotpots, noodles and even miso soup, and it’s used in ponzu, dressings, drinks, sweets and more.

item.title: Oita Toriten: Chicken Tempura — Guide
item.description: Toriten (chicken tempura) is Oita’s beloved soul food, a simple but delicious local speciality found on menus throughout the prefecture. Bite-sized pieces of chicken — usually thigh, sometimes breast — are marinated in a savoury blend of soy sauce, garlic and ginger, then coated in a light tempura batter and deep-fried until golden and crisp on the outside while staying tender and juicy inside. Unlike heavier fried chicken (karaage), toriten has a lighter, airier crust.
